title: Steering policy failure patterns and recovery guidance
body:
Purpose:
This note captures pragmatic failure patterns we've seen when steering/routing decisions diverge from expectations (policy bugs, control-plane split, stale topology, cascading region degradation) and provides concise recovery guidance for first responders and architecture owners. This lives as an operational appendix to the steering architecture docs — think: immediate heuristics + durable architecture notes, not a formal SRE playbook.

Audience and intent:
- Primary: platform oncall and platform engineers responsible for routing and control-plane decisioning.
- Secondary: serving-runtime owners and SREs running multi-region frontends.
- Intent: short, actionable steps to detect, contain, and recover from steering/control-plane incidents with minimal customer impact.

How to use this doc:
- Read the "Quick triage checklist" on pager wakeups.
- If the incident escalates past containment, follow the "Degradation -> rollback decision matrix" and notify the architecture owner.
- After recovery, link the incident to the architecture ticket and schedule a follow-up architecture hardening review.

Quick triage checklist (first 10 minutes)
1) Identify customer impact: Are error rates or latencies visible in the SLO dashboards? (api.latency.p50/p95, downstream 5xx rate).
2) Determine scope: single region, partial region (AZ), cross-region, or global. Check region health panels in Console -> Routing -> Region Health.
3) Check control-plane leader status: controlplane/leader-epoch metric and controlplane.election.count. If >1 leader seen in same region -> suspect split-brain.
4) Validate steering decisions: sampling logs (routing-decision-samples stream) for last 1–5 minutes to see unexpected route target churn.
5) If routing loops or oscillation observed, flip circuit-breaker to hold current active routes (see containment toggles).

Common failure patterns and immediate containment actions
Pattern A: Partial region degradation causing cascading failovers
- Symptom: One AZ shows high queue length and slow token generation; autoscaler triggers many pods but throughput still falls. Observed rise in cross-region traffic and latencies in fallback region.
- Immediate checks: node GPU memory pressure, eviction events, provisioning logs for Dedicated.
- Containment: throttle reroutes by lowering max_burst or temporarily pin traffic to healthy zones in same region (policy override). Enable local-only routing for latency-sensitive customers.
- Recovery: scale up instance pools in degraded AZ OR drain nodes and allow autoscaler to rebalance. If provisioning lag persists, promote healthy zones and announce maintenance window.

Pattern B: Control plane split-brain (leader disagreement across regions)
- Symptom: controlplane.leader_id differs between the control plane replicas; orchestration decisions diverge and inconsistent policy enforcement occurs. Often accompanied by apiserver latency spikes.
- Immediate checks: controlplane.election.count, raft.log.replicas_uptime, network partitions on etcd or internal message bus.
- Containment: set controlplane read-only mode (prevent policy mutations) and promote a single region as authoritative via manual leader override. Route new write requests to authoritative control plane instance.
- Recovery: heal network partition; run log compaction and leader transfer; validate policy convergence via config-hash check across replicas. If automatic reconciliation fails, perform a controlled config push from authoritative region.

Pattern C: Policy regression after canary rollout (incorrect label selectors / precedence bug)
- Symptom: new steering policy introduced; a subset of traffic is misrouted (e.g., failing to prefer low-cost region). Canary metrics show higher error rate and mismatch in expected vs actual targets.
- Immediate checks: policy diff between previous stable and current canary (policy-git diff), canary traffic sample IDs.
- Containment: revert canary using the rollback ID or disable canary routing flag. If Canary is managed by rollout controller, trigger immediate rollback and scale down canary capacity.
- Recovery: revert config, run unit/regression tests in local sim harness for selector precedence, and then re-run a smaller canary with stricter sampling.

Pattern D: Routing loops caused by stale topology or cache staleness
- Symptom: persistent retries and route flapping between two regions; KV cache TTL misaligned with topology updates.
- Immediate checks: topology.version mismatch across edge caches; cache_hitrate drop for prefix-cache and kv-cache-lag.
- Containment: dump and invalidate caches for affected prefixes (cache-invalidate API) or temporarily disable prefix-caching for the disrupted asset class. Flip routing to short-circuit path (direct route) until cache rebuild finishes.
- Recovery: investigate source of stale topology (failed watcher or webhook), fix the watcher, and rehydrate caches by replaying topology snapshots.

Containment toggles (fast actions)
- policy.readOnly=true -> prevents new policy writes (use if control-plane leadership uncertain).
- routing.circuit_breaker.mode=hold -> stop automated failovers and freeze to current active route set.
- routing.region_weight_overrides -> temporary override weights to force local preference.
- cache.invalidate(prefixes=...) -> immediate invalidation for specific keys.
- canary.disable(id=...) -> stops canary traffic.
Note: All toggles must be performed via the Control Plane admin UI or oc/kubectl to the controlplane namespace, and be recorded in the incident log.

Diagnostic commands & quick references
- Check leaders: kubectl -n controlplane exec -it deploy/controlplane-api -- curl localhost:9090/metrics | grep controlplane_leader_id
- List policy revisions: rcli policy list --service=my-service --limit=20
- Dump recent routing decisions: rcli routing tail --since=5m --filter="service:my-service" --output=jsonl > /tmp/routing-sample.jsonl
- Invalidate caches: rcli cache invalidate --prefix=/kv/topology/services/my-service
- Force policy freeze: kubectl -n controlplane set env deploy/controlplane-api policy.readOnly=true

Degradation -> rollback decision matrix
- If customer-facing errors increase > 3x baseline or p95 latency > 2x SLO for > 5 minutes: escalate and prioritize rollback.
- If incident is localized to a single canary or small segment and revertable: perform targeted rollback (canary.disable or policy rollback).
- If incident involves multiple independent failures or control plane split: prefer global freeze (routing.circuit_breaker.mode=hold) and manual staged recovery.
- If recovery action risks data loss (policy mutation rollback removing customer pinned routes): coordinate with Product/Security before full rollback.

Escalation and communication
- Pager to oncall -> #platform-oncall (Slack) and @oncall. Provide: incident short summary, scope (regions), immediate containment toggle used, and next action.
- Notify stakeholders: product owners for affected services, Solutions Eng for high-value customers, Account Exec if >3 enterprise customers impacted.
- Post-incident: file incident summary in confluence (link: confluence:PLATFORM-INCIDENT-ARCHIVE) and tag the architecture ticket for follow-up.

Post-incident analysis checklist
1) Timeline: capture control-plane decisions and routing-sample timeline; attach to the incident.
2) Root cause hypothesis and tests applied.
3) Which containment toggles were used and why.
4) Gaps in observability (metrics/logs/traces) uncovered.
5) Action items: config guardrails, additional canary tests, automation to avoid manual toggles. Assign owners and due dates.

Architectural hardening ideas (to track on a follow-up story)
- Stronger leader arbitration: implement lease-based leader confirmations with cross-region quorum checks.
- Policy pre-checks: run static validation and precedence simulation against a small traffic simulator before canary activation.
- Cache safety: introduce topology revision fencing so caches refuse to serve if revision gap > 2.
- Safe-mode automation: automated short-circuit to read-only mode when quorum loss detected, with an operator confirmation step to change to full freeze.
- Observability: add a dedicated steering-decisions timeline in Console with per-decision correlation ids to speed triage.

Appendix A — Example incident notes (short)
Incident: 2025-01-18 region-west-2 az3 degradation -> cross-region storm
- Impact: p95 latency for embeddings API spiked 4x; affected customers using embeddings-heavy batch flows.
- Containment: set routing.circuit_breaker.mode=hold, applied region_weight_overrides to prefer west-2.az1/az2.
- Recovery: reprovisioned GPU pool, rolled back a buggy autoscaler configuration pushed earlier that caused aggressive scale-in.
- Postmortem actions: tighten autoscaler CPU/GPU probe thresholds, add health check in canary pipeline.

Appendix B — Quick checklist for conference calls
- Start with a one-line summary and scope.
- State containment toggles and who executed them.
- Share the key metrics (error rate, p95 latency, leader count) and their current trend.
- Agree on recovery steps and owners; capture ETA.

Notes and open questions (to resolve in architecture follow-up)
- What should be the maximum allowed topology revision gap before caches reject traffic? (current adhoc: 5 revisions)
- How do we automate safe-mode without increasing blast radius? (proposal: operator confirm within 5 minutes)
- Should policy rollouts require a shadow traffic stage for 24h for high-risk services? (tradeoff: slower rollout vs fewer incidents)

Owners and contacts

- Primary oncall rotation: platform-oncall@redwood.com (see rota in ops/rota)
- SRE lead: Marcus Li
- Product contact for routing: Rosa Montenegro

This document is intentionally compact. For full playbooks, see the SRE runbooks and Confluence incident templates referenced above. Add your incident notes below and link the ticket ID.
